items.question_text: You have deployed an application on a single Compute Engine instance. The application writes logs to disk. Users start reporting errors with the application. You want to diagnose the problem. What should you do?
items.solution_text: Since the application writes logs to disk on a local Compute Engine instance, they are not automatically sent to Cloud Logging. You must first install and configure the Ops Agent (formerly Stackdriver Logging agent) to collect these local log files and forward them to Cloud Logging for centralized analysis.

choices.text: Navigate to Cloud Logging and view the application logs.
Configure a health check on the instance and set a “consecutive successes” Healthy threshold value of 1.
Connect to the instance’s serial console and read the application logs.
Install and configure the Ops agent and view the logs from Cloud Logging.

items.question_text: You recently received a new Google Cloud project with an attached billing account where you will work. You need to create instances, set firewalls, and store data in Cloud Storage. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Google Cloud follows the principle of least privilege by requiring explicit API enablement before resources can be created.
Option B correctly enables the specific APIs needed for Compute Engine (instances and firewalls) and Cloud Storage, adhering to best practices.
Other options are incorrect because enabling all APIs is unnecessary and insecure, while CLI commands in other choices do not properly enable the required services.

choices.text: Use the gcloud CLI services enable cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com command to enable all resources.
Use the gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com command to enable Compute Engine and the gcloud services enable storage-api.googleapis.com command to enable the Cloud Storage APIs.
Open the Google Cloud console and enable all Google Cloud APIs from the API dashboard.
Open the Google Cloud console and run gcloud init --project <project-id> in a Cloud Shell.

items.question_text: Your application development team has created Docker images for an application that will be deployed on Google Cloud. Your team does not want to manage the infrastructure associated with this application. You need to ensure that the application can scale automatically as it gains popularity. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform that eliminates the need to manage underlying infrastructure, directly satisfying the requirement to avoid infrastructure management.
It natively supports automatic scaling of containerized applications based on incoming request volume.
Additionally, Docker images must be stored in Artifact Registry (or Container Registry), making Option D technically accurate compared to Option C which incorrectly suggests Cloud Storage.

choices.text: Create an instance template with the container image, and deploy a Managed Instance Group with Autoscaling.
Upload Docker images to Artifact Registry, and deploy the application on Google Kubernetes Engine using Standard mode.
Upload Docker images to the Cloud Storage, and deploy the application on Google Kubernetes Engine using Standard mode.
Upload Docker images to Artifact Registry, and deploy the application on Cloud Run.

items.question_text: You are migrating a business critical application from your local data center into Google Cloud. As part of your high-availability strategy, you want to ensure that any data used by the application will be immediately available if a zonal failure occurs. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Regional Persistent Disks automatically replicate data synchronously across two zones within a region, ensuring immediate data availability if a single zone fails.
Unlike zonal disks, they do not require snapshots or manual restoration processes to survive a zonal outage.
You can simply create a new VM in the secondary zone and attach the existing regional disk to restore service quickly.

choices.text: Store the application data on a zonal persistent disk. Create a snapshot schedule for the disk. If an outage occurs, create a new disk from the most recent snapshot and attach it to a new VM in another zone.
Store the application data on a zonal persistent disk. If an outage occurs, create an instance in another zone with this disk attached.

Store the application data on a regional persistent disk. Create a snapshot schedule for the disk. If an outage occurs, create a new disk from the most recent snapshot and attach it to a new VM in another zone.
Store the application data on a regional persistent disk. If an outage occurs, create an instance in another zone with this disk attached.

items.question_text: The DevOps group in your organization needs full control of Compute Engine resources in your development project. However, they should not have permission to create or update any other resources in the project. You want to follow Google’s recommendations for setting permissions for the DevOps group. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Google's best practice for IAM is to use predefined roles whenever possible to minimize complexity and maintenance overhead. The `roles/compute.admin` predefined role grants full control over Compute Engine resources, satisfying the primary requirement. Adding `roles/viewer` ensures the group has read access to other project resources (necessary for context) without granting write permissions, thereby strictly adhering to the constraint of not creating or updating non-Compute resources.

Note: While custom roles (Option C) are technically valid for least privilege, they cannot be defined at the folder level (a technical impossibility in GCP IAM), making that option incorrect. Basic roles like `roles/editor` (Option D) are too broad, and basic roles combined with predefined ones (Option A) is the standard exam pattern for this specific constraint scenario despite some community debate about custom roles being 'more' granular.

choices.text: Grant the basic role roles/viewer and the predefined role roles/compute.admin to the DevOps group.
Create an IAM policy and grant all compute.instanceAdmin.* permissions to the policy. Attach the policy to the DevOps group.
Create a custom role at the folder level and grant all compute.instanceAdmin.* permissions to the role. Grant the custom role to the DevOps group.
Grant the basic role roles/editor to the DevOps group.
